title: Rep2Text: Decoding Full Text from a Single LLM Token Representation
claim: A single hidden state from one model is projected by a learned adapter into a second model's input space to regenerate the source text.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, dashed link zooming hidden state into adapter
description: Three dashed-border panels read left to right. The left panel shows the target model M: a stack of embedding layer, a Transformer layer with Self-Attention, Add & Normalize and Feed Forward blocks, and an unembedding layer, all in blue. Token inputs such as 'Omaha High School ( Arkansas )' enter at the bottom. The last-token hidden state is drawn as a dashed green box, and a thin dashed line carries it to the middle panel. The middle panel shows the decoding model M'. A yellow trapezoid labeled Adapter takes the hidden state h_l, and an embedding layer and tokenizer handle the system and user prompts. Both feed Transformer layers and an unembedding layer, which output the reconstructed tokens 'Northside High School ( Arkansas )'. The right panel expands the Adapter in green, with LayerNorm, a gated mixture of transformation matrices and a small MLP. The eye goes first to the yellow Adapter.
caption: Overview of Rep2Text. The last-token representation obtained from the $l$-th layer of the target model $\mathcal{M}$ is projected into the embedding space of the decoding model $\mathcal{M}^\prime$ via the adapter. The projected embeddings, together with those of the system and the user prompts, are then fed into the decoding model to reconstruct the corresponding text sequence.
abstract: Large language models represent text as hidden numerical patterns, but what information these representations actually contain remains a mystery. Can we recover the original text from just one of them? In this paper, we introduce Rep2Text, a method designed to answer this question by reconstructing text from a single hidden representation. We find that these representations preserve much more information than we might expect. For short texts of about 16 words, Rep2Text can recover roughly half of the original words while preserving their overall meaning. As the text gets longer, recovering the exact wording becomes harder, but the main ideas can still be recovered. These findings offer a new way to understand what language models store internally and highlight potential privacy risks, as hidden representations may reveal parts of the original input.
